statements.quote: It also treats OCD, and it is likely to be able to treat other conditions as well.
statements.context: Background paragraph on transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) in a post celebrating Cigna's national adolescent-depression TMS coverage policy. The author states TMS treats depression and OCD and expects it to treat further conditions.
statements.confidence_phrase: is likely to be able to
statements.note: Open-ended efficacy expectation; no named condition or date.

statements.quote: insurance tends to follow the FDA and will rarely approve treatments in broader populations than the FDA was willing to sign off on.
statements.context: Explaining why the Neuronetics adolescent (15+) FDA label matters: insurers follow FDA labels and will rarely cover populations broader than the label.
statements.note: Generalization about payer behavior; borderline truism.

statements.quote: I'm am here to encourage my colleagues at all health plans to update their coverage policy promptly, because not only is it not keeping with the evidence, nor with the FDA approval, but frankly, it opens them up to tremendous liability
statements.context: The Cigna/Evernorth policy requires failure of two antidepressant trials for ages 15-17 before covering TMS, which the FDA label does not require. The author says this exposes health plans to tremendous liability.
statements.note: Borderline: present liability exposure implying future legal consequences; opens with advice to update policies.

statements.quote: If you're an insurance company, do you really want to be in the position of demanding that the children take drugs that have a risk of suicidal thoughts before we offer them a treatment that doesn't have a risk of increased suicidality? Because what does that sound like? It is a lawsuit waiting to happen.
statements.context: Cigna/Evernorth's adolescent TMS policy demands two failed antidepressant trials (drugs carrying the FDA black-box suicidality warning) before TMS, which has no such warning. The author predicts this requirement will produce a lawsuit.
statements.note: Legal-consequence forecast tied to a coverage policy; earlier in the post the same requirement is called 'asking for trouble'.

statements.quote: Does anyone on earth think Owen Muir, M.D., your author, will not be called an expert witness in such a legal matter? Or will this article documenting the risk-benefit profile of these two treatments not be included in the evidence ? Is there any chance anyone at your insurance company subscribes to this newsletter? Is this going to show up in discovery? Of course, it will be.
statements.context: Following the lawsuit prediction: the author expects to be called as an expert witness and expects this article to appear in discovery in such a case.
statements.note: Conditional on the predicted lawsuit; rhetorical questions answered by the author.

statements.quote: Once the extremely predictable lawsuit happens, I can go to discovery, find this article in an inbox, find the proof that it was opened, and then prove that they knew this was a problem well before my lawsuit.
statements.context: The author speaks in the voice of a hypothetical class-action ERISA attorney who forwards this article to insurers; he calls a lawsuit over the adolescent TMS coverage requirement extremely predictable.
statements.note: Hypothetical attorney voice; restates the lawsuit call.

statements.quote: This covered policy is an excellent step in the right direction, but I also think it's a time bomb.
statements.context: Verdict on Cigna/Evernorth's new adolescent TMS coverage policy: progress, but the two-antidepressant-trial requirement is a 'time bomb' for future liability.
statements.note: Metaphorical forecast of future liability; the author adds it is easy to defuse by covering TMS with standard of care.

statements.quote: I did a rewrite of the CIGNA/Evernorth coverage policy to avoid this series of angry and very sympathetic parent lawsuits and predictably withering coverage in the NY Times and WSJ that would inevitably follow
statements.context: Introducing the author's proposed rewrite of the Cigna/Evernorth TMS policy (no prior medication failure for ages 15-18). He predicts that, absent such changes, parent lawsuits and harsh NYT/WSJ coverage would inevitably follow.
statements.note: Conditional on the policy staying as written; compound claim (lawsuits and press coverage).

statements.quote: For those health plans, I think they're even more exposed to liability, not only for a coverage policy that adds additional risk, but for ERISA fiduciary breach.
statements.context: Closing: health plans with no adolescent TMS coverage at all are, in the author's view, even more exposed to liability than Cigna, including ERISA fiduciary breach, now that a major plan covers it.
statements.note: Borderline: present-state liability exposure implying future claims against other payers.

statements.quote: I’ll do a version I narrate soon enough, I suspect.
statements.context: Aside in a podcast plug: the author's book was turned into an Amazon audiobook; he expects to produce a self-narrated version.
statements.note: Own-activity plan; low forecast value. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: one could imagine an almost infinite variety of stimulation patterns that are individually tailored per person, and we are absolutely not there yet.
statements.context: Survey of TMS stimulation patterns (1 Hz, 10 Hz, theta burst, Quadra pulse). The author implies individually tailored stimulation is a future destination not yet reached.
statements.note: Borderline: implicit expectation of future personalization ('not there yet'); no explicit call or date.

statements.quote: tomorrow’s issue is a podcast—it tell the more full story of how iTBS came to be, and where it is going…do I switch to iTBS as a First Line option?
statements.context: End of Part I of an essay on when new evidence should change practice, focused on intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS) versus 10 Hz TMS. The author announces a podcast issue the next day and leaves open whether he will adopt iTBS first-line.
statements.note: Publishing schedule for the author's own newsletter (CONTROL candidate). The first-line iTBS question is posed, not answered.

statements.quote: Ampa sponsors Rapid Acting Mental Health Treatment on May 18th, in Los Angeles.
statements.context: Podcast blurb on iTBS with Carlene MacMillan, Will Sauve and Jonathan Downar. Plug for the author's RAMHT event on May 18 (2025) in Los Angeles, sponsored by Downar's company Ampa Health.

statements.quote: they're going to be regular articles coming out of this feed, but they're not going be every day, and the reason they're not gonna be every day is because if I do it this way, they will be better.
statements.context: The author ends nearly two years of daily publishing. He commits to regular but less-than-daily articles and predicts they will be better.
statements.note: Newsletter cadence commitment; CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: I may have something to say close to every day, and I really enjoy writing every day, but I'm not gonna click publish every day.
statements.context: Same cadence change: the author will keep writing but will not publish daily.
statements.note: Restatement of the cadence change within the same post; CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: I'm going to write more audacious articles, I'm going to encourage more along form contributions from collaborators, and this is gonna be a better newsletter, a great newsletter, not just a daily newsletter.
statements.context: Plans after dropping the daily cadence: more ambitious long-form articles, more collaborator contributions, and a prediction that the newsletter will be better.
statements.note: Qualitative own-newsletter plan; CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: Part of the commitment means I'm gonna make it better, and that means writing more audacious articles, and that means less frequent publication.
statements.context: Closing restatement of the plan: better newsletter, more audacious articles, less frequent publication.
statements.note: Restatement of the preceding plan; CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: And I must pause till it gets reinstated by the grace of Trump, and my following, thusly restored.
statements.context: Closing line of a Julius Caesar parody eulogy for TikTok, written when TikTok was banned in the US. The speaker expects TikTok to be reinstated through Trump and his following restored. The post's introduction says the ban was lifted before the poem could be published.
statements.note: Satirical framing but the reinstatement expectation reads as sincere. Per the intro, TikTok was already restored at the post date, so the call was resolved before publication.

statements.quote: Rapid Acting Mental Health Treatment returns! Our next live-action newsletter event is on May 18th, along with the APA meeting in Los Angeles.

statements.quote: UHG is closing HBMC and Optum at Home by end of month. We were told in a scripted meeting today.
statements.context: Quoted insider source, whose identity and employment the author says he confirmed: UnitedHealth Group is closing HBMC (home based medical care) and Optum at Home by end of April 2025. Post dated 2025-04-13; title hedges with 'May Be Shutting Down'.

statements.quote: Some will be moved into other positions. The rest will get let go 4/24 I’m told.
statements.context: Same insider source on the Optum at Home / HBMC closure: some staff redeployed, the rest laid off on April 24, 2025. The source adds that PTO was removed for that day.

statements.quote: Legacy Optum at Home patients will remain, these are… external contracts. This will happen by end of month and they will have more details in the coming weeks.

statements.quote: I’ve heard the redeployment will happen for some but no idea how many.
statements.context: Same insider source: some Optum at Home / HBMC staff will be redeployed within UHG; headcount unknown.

statements.quote: I hope this next round of layoffs is conducted with compassion and in keeping with the law.

statements.quote: The path from the underground to legitimate treatment runs not through it all over again , but upward. We need ever more rigorous studies by endlessly more buttoned up scientists.
statements.context: After MDMA phase 3 papers were retracted for investigator misconduct, the author (who kept his MDMA review in print with a warning) says MDMA can only become a legitimate treatment through more rigorous, independent studies.
statements.note: Borderline: prescriptive path statement about MDMA's route to legitimacy; no explicit prediction of approval or timing.

statements.quote: I just want to remind my readers I called “short selling” united as a strategy way back on April 7, 2023
statements.context: Victory lap: the author recalls his April 7, 2023 piece that (with heavy disclaimers) suggested short selling UnitedHealth; UNH is now at $454 after a 22% one-day fall, so the trade would be 'in the money'. No new forward horizon is stated.

statements.quote: Legal cannabis means that all the people who were kept away from cannabis by its criminal status might begin using cannabis now. Even old people. It makes the cannabis market—and thus the range of those who ingest it—bigger.
statements.context: Framing for two Ontario cohort papers (JAMA Neurology, JAMA Network Open) on cannabis-related acute care, dementia and 5-year mortality. The author expects legalization to expand cannabis use and the user base, including older adults.
statements.note: Mechanistic expectation about legalization and use; partly describes a trend the cited data already show.

statements.quote: We’re gonna need to understand this risk factor in more detail in older adults, especially as cannabis products become increasingly legal and increasingly common.
statements.context: Closing of the cannabis review: the author expects cannabis products to become increasingly legal and common, and says the dementia/mortality risk in older adults will need more study.
statements.note: Compound: research need (normative) plus a trend expectation that cannabis becomes more legal and common.
